description: Team FARMONAUTS, (2025 NASA Space Apps Global Nominees), tackles "Field Shift." Our tool, KRISHI (Knowledge-based Rotation Insights for Soil, Harvest & Irrigation), is a mobile-friendly, English + Bangla-supported tool that uses NASA Earth observation data and local soil information to recommend climate-resilient crop rotations that improve soil health and save water for Bangladeshi farmers and extension workers.
summary: CropOrbit is a free Bangla and English web app that turns 45 years of NASA POWER climate data into a plain answer for farmers in all 64 districts of Bangladesh: has the rain timing for Aman, Aus or Boro really shifted, or is it just a bad year? A farmer picks a district on a 3D globe, and CropOrbit compares two periods of the daily NASA record and tests whether any change is reliable. It then says so plainly, including “no reliable shift, keep your usual calendar”, and writes a short Bangla SMS for any phone. It also includes a rule-based Farm helper for common crop questions and a clearly labelled, simulated smart-irrigation demo.
details:
The challenge it answers-

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. Farmers face shifting temperatures, unpredictable rain and water shortages, yet satellite records are hard to use. CropOrbit turns that record into one clear, honest answer per district, so a wrong guess about the season costs less.

How it works-

Choose an area: the farmer opens a 3D globe with NASA Blue Marble imagery, or searches, and picks one of 64 districts. The site runs in Bangla or English.

NASA data: it reads daily NASA POWER (MERRA-2) data from 1981 to the latest days. Each district uses its grid cell, which is about 50 km wide.

Planting-window check: it compares the median rain-timing dates of two periods (for example 1998–2011 against 2012–2025) for Aman, Aus and Boro, and tests whether the shift is reliable. It also re-checks with a longer record, a stricter setting, a looser setting, and whether the direction flips. A shift is reported only if it holds.

Honest labels: each result shows reliable or not reliable, with p-values and a “How we checked” table. The site warns that testing 64 districts will flag a few by chance.

Local signals: it also shows rain in the last 7 and 30 days against the usual amount, temperature change per decade, days at 35 °C or above, and winter-night warming.

Farmer-ready output: a short Bangla SMS message, plus a Farm helper that answers 20 common crop questions (rule-based, no AI).

Field-control demo (simulated): sensors send readings through a radio gateway to a control centre, which switches a pump on, stops it at the target moisture, and sends the farmer an SMS. The NASA rain signal changes the trigger: with only 23 mm of rain against a usual 202 mm in Sunamganj, irrigation starts at 65% soil moisture instead of 60%. Every number here is simulated and labelled so.

Limits we state openly

NASA data is regional, not field-level. The newest days are provisional. Advice is a signal to check with a local agriculture officer, not an instruction.

What we’d build next

A crop-rotation comparison (at least three strategies) with evidence, benefits and risksMore NASA data: SMAP soil moisture, GPM rainfall and MODIS vegetation healthA real field pilot with ESP32 sensors and an actual SMS linkTesting the results with farmers and agriculture officersAn installable offline mobile app
